The Triśikhibrāhmaṇopaniṣad. "That which is full... thus [ends] the peace mantra. The Brāhmaṇa Section.
Regarding the subject of the Self and Brahman, there were questions.
Triśikhī Brāhmaṇa went to the world of Āditya; having gone there, he said to him: "O Blessed One, what is the body? What is the vital breath? What is the cause? What is the Self? (1)
I am the Supreme Brahman, radiant as the reality of Śiva, perfectly established through the singular knowledge of Yoga, and entirely free from all counter-correlates.

Here indeed unfolds this *Triśikhībrāhmaṇopaniṣad*, which is a division of the White Yajurveda; it culminates in Brahman alone, which is without a second, and it illuminates the expansion of the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) that serves as the means to attain it. Of that [Upaniṣad]...
The commentary is now begun from a very brief text.

This narrative, consisting of a dialogue in the form of questions and answers between the Brahmin Triśikhī and Āditya, is intended for the purpose of praising this knowledge (*vidyā*). To the question "What is this narrative?", he says: "Triśikhī," by name.

Triśikhī—a Brahmin, the offspring of Brahmā, a sage named Sanātana—having approached the Sun, the seat of the Ādityas, according to the prescribed rite, asked: "What is the cause of the body, the vital breaths, and so forth? Or what is its own nature? || 1 ||
(117) "The state of Śiva belongs to everything.
He said: "Know that all this is indeed Śiva alone. However, Śiva—the eternal, pure, stainless, omnipresent, non-dual bliss—is one; having created all this by his own light, he [shines forth]."

The unity [of the Self and Brahman] is like that of a heated iron ball; though one, it appears as if divided. If it is asked what it is that illumines this [appearance], it is said: it is Brahman, denoted by the word "Being" (sat), which is variegated by ignorance (avidyā). || 2 ||

Having accepted that question, the Blessed One said to him: "What is it?"—"All this," and so forth. Whatever you have asked, such as "Is it the body? and so on, know that to be Śiva alone, because everything is imagined through the ignorance of Śiva. This is so because [the world] is the locus of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

To the objection that [the Self] might be subject to impermanence and other such flaws, he says: "But what? The web of conceptual constructions imagined by one who is ignorant of his own nature is indeed defiled by defects such as impermanence; however, the substrate of those conceptualizations—the non-dual Self, Śiva alone, characterized by attributes such as permanence—is never [so defiled].

The meaning is that it attains the state of duality. In response to the doubt—by whom was the entire collection of conceptual constructions (vikalpa) imagined, and what is that which illuminates them so that they attain oneness—it is said: That one Śiva, having created all this by his own splendor, becomes one with it like a heated iron ball.

He says that it also appears as distinct from that [the Self], using the word "by its own" (*svena*). Having attained unity, it appears as if divided through the perspective of one's own knower. To the question "What is that?", in response to the inquiry in the *Triśikhī-brahma-upaniṣad* beginning with "Is it the body?", regarding that which was asserted—namely, that "all this is indeed Śiva"—[it is said:]...

With reference to the effect imagined by oneself, he clarifies one’s own causality and the fact that the unmanifest (avyakta) and so forth, distinct from oneself, are the effects—by the word "Being" (sat). The meaning is that, as it is said, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," its variegated nature arises through connection with its own ignorance, while its state as Brahman is established by its own true form. || 2 ||
The origin of the entire world is from Brahman;

from Brahman comes the unmanifest (avyakta); from the unmanifest, the great principle (mahat); from the great principle, the ego (ahaṃkāra); from the ego, the five subtle elements (tanmātras); and from the five subtle elements, the five gross elements (mahābhūtas).
The entire world [arises] from the five great elements. || 3 ||

(118) Since the absolute Brahman (*kevalabrahman*), being devoid of any locus for conceptualization, is free from all counter-correlates and non-conceptual, let that remain as it is; however, regarding the qualified Brahman (*śabalabrahman*), what is it that is conceptualized? To this he says: "The unmanifest [is] of Brahman. As to the question, "What follows from that?"—

From the Unmanifest (avyakta), which has attained a state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmyabhāva), arises the Great One (mahat). From the Great One, having attained the state of sattva, arises the ego (ahaṃkāra). From the ego, having attained the state of rajas, arise the five subtle elements (pañcatanmātrāṇi).
From the five subtle elements, in which tamas predominates, arise the five gross elements (pañcamahābhūtāni).
The meaning is that they have been quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*).
From the five great elements, which have been quintuplicated and are subordinate to the three qualities (*guṇa*) with *tamas* as the predominant factor, the entire universe [arises]. || 3 ||

Why is it that a single mass is divided into many parts? It is because of the division of the modifications of the elements (*bhūta-vikāra*). How does the division of the modifications of the elements occur within a single mass? It occurs by way of the distinction between cause and effect.

There are distinctions regarding the portions (aṃśa), the principles (tattva), the denotators and the denoted (vācaka-vācya), the locations (sthāna), the objects (viṣaya), the deities (devatā), and the divisions of the treasury (kośabheda). || 4 ||

Regarding how the world, which is of a single unified nature (*piṇḍātman*), can be "entire" (*akhila*), [the answer is] that it is due to the division of the transformations of the five gross elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) through quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*). To this, he raises an objection with the words "in one," and explains the manner of that [division] with the words "that. [This refers to] the fact that earth and the other elements are effects of space (*ākāśa*).

The division of the five elements, beginning with earth, occurs through the differentiation of cause and effect among those respective elements— namely, that space and the others are the causes of earth and the rest. Furthermore, they are distinguished by the differentiation of their principles (tattvas) as the ear and so forth,

which are portions of space and the other elements, and by the differentiation of the respective locations of their physical seats (golaka), based on the distinction between the signifier and the signified.

There are manifold divisions according to the distinctions of objects such as sound and so forth, according to the distinctions of deities of the quarters and so forth, and according to the distinctions of sheaths such as bliss and māyā. The meaning is that within the single mass of the egg of ignorance (avidyāṇḍa), the various divisions of the elements and their derivatives are logically established. || 4 ||
The divisions of the parts of space and the other elements are as follows:
space consists of the internal organ, mind, intellect, thought, and ego; air consists of the samāna, udāna, vyāna, apāna, and prāṇa breaths; fire consists of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.

Water consists of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Earth consists of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. (p. 119) Thus, he clarifies the meaning of what was stated in the aphorism according to the sequence beginning with ether, starting with the words "Now," and so forth. This means the components of ether. Now, the components of air and the others are described:
"Wind," thus [it is said]. || 5 ||
Their specific objects—
namely cognition, conceptualization, determination, reflection, and self-identification— are the domain of the internal organ, which is an effect of space.
Equalizing, elevating, grasping, cooking, and exhalation are the functions of air, having as their objects the organs of action.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the objects of the organs of knowledge, which are the effects of fire and are supported by water.
Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and sexual pleasure are the objects of the organs of action, which are the effects of earth.
The objects of the vital breaths and the subtle elements are included within the objects of the organs of action and the organs of knowledge;
the mind and the intellect include the thinking faculty and the ego-sense.
Having stated the distinctions among the parts, he states the distinctions among the objects: "jñāna... (verse 6).

The subtle elements (tanmātras), which consist of mere atoms, are the objects of the individual soul; they are most subtle, and their perception consists of the visualization and mental integration of space and the other [subtle qualities]. || 7 ||
The subtle elements alone are said to be "space," etc. (7).
The division into internal and so forth is as follows:
thus, the twelve factors are internal (*ādhyātmika*), external (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*ādhidaivika*).
In this regard, [the deities corresponding to the factors] are the Moon, the Four-faced One (Brahmā), the Directions, Vāyu, the Sun, Varuṇa, Aśvin, Agni, Indra, Upendra, Prajāpati, and Yama.
The very vital breaths (prāṇas), which have entered within the twelve channels in the form of the presiding deities of the sense organs, are the limbs;
the knowledge of those limbs is itself the "Knower" (jñātṛ). || 8 ||

(120) "By way of the division into parts and so forth" refers to the phrase "thus, etc. Here, [the term] *ādhyātmika* (pertaining to the self) and so forth are used because they exist with reference to the self (*ātman*), the body, the collection of elements (*bhūtajāta*), and the collection of deities (*devatājāta*). Among those, the *ādhyātmika* and *ādhibhautika* have already been explained; here, however, there is the intention to speak of the *adhidaivika* (pertaining to the divine).
The presiding deities of the instruments are mentioned here: the twelve channels beginning with Iḍā.

The meaning is that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is the knowledge of all limbs, becomes the knower—the individual soul (jīva)—precisely when it identifies itself with that [organ] as its limiting adjunct (upādhi). || 8 ||
The manifestation of the activity of the knower,

as well as the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) of ether, air, fire, water, and earth, occurs as follows: through the common conjunction [of the elements], the quality of sound— which constitutes the state of being a knower— is situated in space (*ākāśa*), presided over by speech and perceived through the ear.

Space remains [in the heart]. Through the yoga of vyāna, the quality of touch, presided over by the hands, remains in the air via the skin; the air remains. Through the yoga of udāna, the quality of form, presided over by the feet, remains in fire via the eyes; the fire remains.

Through the yoga of leading the mind, the quality of taste, presided over by the tongue and situated in the genitals, abides in water; thus water abides. Through the yoga of the vital breath, egoity, the quality of smell, presided over by the sense of smell and situated in the anus, abides in earth;
thus earth abides. One who knows it thus truly knows. 9.

Having thus examined the threefold suffering, beginning with that which is internal, he now clarifies the activity of the knower as manifested through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), starting with the word "atha" (now).
"Pañcīkaraṇa" means the state of being a knower produced by the process of quintuplication; this is the meaning.

He describes the activity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), who serve as the substrata for the superimposition of the phenomenal world both individually and collectively, as well as their entry into the elements and their effects, in the verse beginning with "jñātṛtva" (the state of being a knower).

[The Lord] supports both the *jīva* and the *īśvara*, [bestowing upon them] the state of being a knower, and so forth; having become the ether and so on, He abides within the ether and other elements.

The meaning is that he "abides. Thus, one who knows—namely, one who knows the inner ruler (antaryāmin) as being unattached to the five elements and their effects—becomes that inner ruler; this is the remainder of the sense. (p. 121) [This is the portion of the mantra.]
From Brahman proceeds the creation up to the stage of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*).
On this subject, there are these verses: "The sixteen parts, having become distinct, [merge] their own half-portions into the others in succession."
In the sequence of the internal organ, the vyāna breath, the eyes, the tongue, the anus, and space; || 1 ||
In each and every element, there are four primary [parts] according to their eastern and northern portions;
first resorting to space, it is established within earth and the other elements.
The primary [state] is to be known as the supreme (parā) above; they know the others as the unsurpassed (anuttarā).
Thus a portion arose from that, and likewise a portion arose from those. || 3 ||
Therefore, since they are woven together, one depending on the other, in successive order,
he says "here" to show that the very meaning which was stated by the Brāhmaṇa is also restated by the mantras.
From the collection of the sixteen kalās and their effects imagined as separate by one's own ignorance (svājñā),

[one realizes] the seedless, partless Brahman— which appears distinct from that collection through the vision of one who knows (svajña)— by means of the vision of one's own ignorance which sustains all such mental constructs.

Having first been conceptualized as seeds in the form of the kalās ending with the names of prāṇa and so forth as recited in the Praśnopaniṣad, and having become the Lord (Īśvara) through union with the Lord who is the substrate for their own superimposition—the word "internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa) denotes its cause, space (ākāśa); the word "vyāna" denotes air (vāyu); and by the word "eye" [is denoted]...

Agni, because of its fiery nature, corresponds to the sense of taste (*rasa*), while water corresponds to the word "anus" (*pāyu*) and earth to the word "anus"; thus, following the sequence of space— that is, the sequence beginning with ether—
one should assign the supreme half-portions, the primary constituents of the five elements, respectively to each respective element.
Having deposited [the portions] || 1 ||— by means of the eastern and northern parts, beginning with space (*ākāśa*) and ending with earth (*pṛthivī*),

because the respective half-portions of each element have been deposited into that very element— one should divide the remaining half-portions four times each; thus, space [deposits] its own portion and the other half-portions.
Having cast [the portions] into the four elements beginning with air, in the same way, air casts its own half and the other half-portion into space, fire, water, and earth;
the rest is the same as previously described. Thus, when the fivefold compounding (pañcīkaraṇa) has been accomplished, [as it was] before—

That portion which exists depending upon space remains established within earth and the other elements after the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa). || 2 || It should be understood that, prior to this, those respective primary portions of each element are the "parās" (supreme) or most excellent;

for even when the elements have been quintuplicated, they are designated by the name of the predominant element, according to the principle: "But on account of the predominance [of one element], there is the designation of that. (Brahma Sūtra 2.4.22).
In accordance with the Sūtras of Vyāsa, its supremacy is justified by the designation of those respective elements.

"The others" means the secondary parts other than the primary ones; "those who know them" refers to those who understand this. Since it thus consists of parts of the five elements, therefore, from those primary parts, in that manner...

The secondary portion (gauṇāṃśa) came into being. Regarding the reading "the portions of the five elements came into being, the secondary portions came into being," the word *abhūt* is used in the sense of *abhūvan* (they came into being), which is a grammatical modification of the verb. 3. Since this is so, therefore, in due order, [it is] woven lengthwise and crosswise within the five elements.
The meaning is that the secondary parts exist by mutually depending upon the primary parts which are radiant with their own essential qualities.
The creation of the universe consisting of the moving and the unmoving is composed of the five elements; that earth is endowed with consciousness.

From that [earth] come herbs and food; from those, the four kinds of funeral cakes (piṇḍas); and from them, the bodily constituents (dhātus): chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. || 5 ||
Some say that, through connection with those [elements], the bodily aggregates arise from the elements in certain places;
therein, the food-made aggregate is situated in the region of the navel.
In its center is the heart, like the interior of a lotus bud with its stalk;
within it dwell the deities who possess the consciousness of agency and ego.
Its seed is a mass of darkness, consisting of delusion, inert and dense;
it exists residing in the throat, and from this the world has become intermingled.
The Self, whose nature is the bliss of return, situated in the supreme state at the crown of the head,
endowed with infinite power, shines forth in the form of the universe.

(123) Thus, regarding the statement that "from the fivefold-composed elements joined with consciousness, [the world] is born," he says— starting with "pañca"— that the universe consisting of the moving and the unmoving is born. From that [source], presided over by consciousness— that is, from the *ātman* presided over by *caitanya*— [beings] arise in four ways, distinguished as *jarāyuja* (viviparous) and so forth.
The meaning is that "lumps" (piṇḍas) have been produced. He states that even the elements (dhātus) arise from food alone—beginning with the word "rasa" (in verse 5).
He says "some" (kecit) to indicate that only some [authorities] maintain this view. "From their conjunction" (tadyogataḥ) means from the conjunction of semen and blood;
thus the lumps arise from the semen and blood produced by the elements of the person who has consumed the food.

Some say they are "piṇḍas" (lumps); the meaning is that they consist entirely of food (*annamaya*). To the question, "Where does a lump, which is the essence of food, find a place? he says: "In that" (*tasmin*).

[It resides] in that aggregate of elements (*bhūtakadamba*), because it is the cause of the life of all living beings. (6) To the question, "What exists in the midst of that? he says: "Of this" (*asya*).
Regarding that which consists of food (*annamaya*): to the question of what exists depending upon that, he says—“sattva,” etc.

Devas such as Indra and others, as well as Brahmā and others, exist within *sattva*, being dominated by the quality of *sattva*. Alternatively, the deities are those conscious agents of ego (*kartṛ-ahaṃkāra-cetanāḥ*), characterized by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The meaning is that the sense organs exist. (7) To the question, "What is the seed of the heart? he says: "of this. The meaning is that it is dense self-ignorance (*svājñāna*). To the question, "Where does that reside? he says: "it resides. According to the Śruti, self-ignorance has the mind as its location, extending to the throat; thus, [he says] "the throat."

The mind, having taken its seat in the throat, functions there. By means of that mind, which is overwhelmed by its own ignorance, this world becomes mixed with and pervaded by it. (8) To the question, "If the world is mixed with one's own ignorance, why does it appear in the form of the world? he says: "The inner self... [and so on]. Of the world...

Although it is pervaded by its own knowledge, according to the scripture stating that "the Fourth (Turiya) is situated at the crown," the Self— whose nature is inner bliss— having become firmly seated in the supreme state at the place of the crown which is untouched by its own ignorance, and being endowed with infinite power as the very Self of the Lord, manifests in the form of the universe.

Since this is so, therefore the manifestation even in the form of the world is grounded in the inner self (pratyagātman) and does not reside in ignorance or the world which is its effect; such is the meaning. || 9 ||
The four states exist everywhere: waking exists in waking; deep sleep and the fourth state exist [in waking], but never in any other states whatsoever. (10)
Pervading all places, possessing four forms, and having Śiva as its essence, it is like the great fruit in which all juices are present and which impels everything. (11)
In the very same way, within the sheath composed of food, the other sheaths reside.
As is the sheath, so is the individual soul (jīva); as is the individual soul, so is Śiva.
Likewise, the individual soul (jīva) is subject to modification, while Śiva is changeless;
those sheaths are his modifications, for they are the agents that operate throughout the various states.
Just as foam arises from the churning of the ocean of nectar,
so too do many conceptual constructions arise solely from the churning of the mind.

He describes the four states produced by the manifestation of the world and the nature of the conscious substrate (cid-dhātu) that illumines them, beginning with the words "everywhere" (sarvatra). The waking state exists everywhere within the phenomenal world (prapañca) manifested by the Witness (sākṣin), because of the activity of the entire collection of organs.

Because it is possible to understand this clearly: the meaning is that within the sheath composed of food (annamaya-kośa), just as in the sheath of vital breath (prāṇamaya-kośa) and the others, the triad beginning with the waking state (jāgrat) exists, but not in the other states. || 10 ||

He states that the state of waking is the substratum for dreams and so forth, and that this [substratum-hood] resides in the Lord (Īśvara), who is the locus of one's own superimposition— by the word "all" (*sarva*).
[The Lord exists] in the form of Viśva, Virāṭ, Otr, and so on, up to the non-conceptual state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*).

The meaning is that the inner self (pratyagātman) always exists as the thread woven through all states, such as waking and so forth, whether in their individual or collective aspects. But how is it that the inner self is woven through everything? To this, he establishes its all-pervasive nature by means of the analogies of the sheaths and the living being, using the word "just as" (yathā). Just as...

The *annamaya-kośa* (the sheath composed of food) is the support of all sheaths and is pervasive; likewise is the *jīva*. Just as the *ātman* exists pervading all the modifications of the sheaths preceded by the conceit of "I" and "mine," so too does Śiva exist, remaining untouched by those modifications. This is the state of being with modification (*savikāratva*) and being without modification (*nirvikāratva*) of the *jīva* and Śiva respectively.
[It is] established upon the existence or non-existence of the conceit regarding the sheaths (kośa). Why?

Because the conceptualization of the three states, their causes, the five sheaths, and so forth, has arisen—just like the foam from the vessel of essence produced by churning—in this way, through the churning of the mind, the waking state and the others come to exist.
Thus, from volition (saṃkalpa) alone, many such conceptual constructions (vikalpa) arise; the meaning is that in the absence of mental volition, nothing at all exists. || 14 ||
The movement of the southern and northern solstices proceeds by means of karma; the agent of karma attains peace through its abandonment.
When this southern [solstice] is reached, one has gone toward the world of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*). (15)
Through the conceit of egoism, Sadāśiva indeed becomes the individual soul (jīva);
and through association with Prakṛti, characterized by non-discrimination, he becomes deluded therein.
Having gone through hundreds of various wombs, it sleeps under the influence of latent impressions;
yet through liberation, it moves back and forth just as a fish moves between two banks.
Then, by the power of time alone, through the discernment of self-knowledge,
he turned toward the north and proceeded from one place to another in succession.
Having fixed his vital breaths (prāṇas) at the crown of the head, remaining established in the practice of yoga, he proceeds;
thus, through various actions born of mental resolve, the embodied soul (jīva), being a doer, exists bound without respiration by the snare of saṃsāra imagined by the mind. As long as...

Through its own ignorance, it attains the state of having a self-nature and thus transmigrates. When this [self] abandons both its own ignorance and its effects through its own knowledge (*svajñāna*), then it shall attain the cessation of the delusion that is distinct from itself. Having raised the doubt as to how the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) arises for Śiva, or the state of being Śiva for the living soul, [the text addresses] the non-self (*anātman*).
He says "in the course" (ayane) to show that through the conceit of self, Śiva becomes a *jīva*, and through the abandonment of that conceit, the *jīva* becomes Śiva;
[this occurs] in the course of performing rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta*, which are composed of desires, volitions, and the like, devoid even of the scent of knowledge.

When the southern [path] is reached || 15–17 || When does the individual soul (jīva) become Śiva? What is the means for attaining its true nature? To this he says: "Then" (tataḥ). Then, through the grace of the Lord resulting from the dedication of the fruits of performed virtuous deeds with a desireless mind, having turned toward the north (the path of liberation),...

The meaning is that, starting from the passage "they attain the flame" (te 'rciṣam abhisaṃbhavanti), having reached one place after another, he gradually attains the state of the variegated Brahman (śabalabrahmapada). What does he do while becoming oriented toward the north? To this, he says:

"Upon the head" (mūrdhni): the yogi, seated upon the *siddha* and other seats, having placed his own vital breaths (*prāṇas*) at the head by way of the *suṣumnā* channel, constantly practicing the yoga exercise, pierces the skull at the prescribed time and, proceeding by the path of the gods (*devayāna*), reaches the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). He does not [return].
The meaning is that he returns again.
Knowledge that brings about immediate liberation arises from yoga; from knowledge, yoga proceeds. (19)
The yogi who is constantly devoted to the knowledge of yoga does not perish;
he perceives Śiva as abiding within all modifications, yet those modifications do not abide in Śiva.
Having stated that one should meditate with single-minded devotion upon the illuminator of yoga through various yogic practices—
that the fruit of the performance of mere ritual action is the lunar station (candrapada),
whereas the fruit of the performance of the combined practice of action and knowledge is the attainment of the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka)— he said:
He states the means for the knowledge of the undifferentiated (nirviśeṣajñāna), which brings about immediate liberation (sadyaḥkaivalya): "From yoga" (yogāt).

Through the practice of hearing all the Vedāntas—performed by one who possesses the fourfold means, such as the constant performance of the duties of one's own stage of life (svāśramācāra)—the knowledge of the undifferentiated arises.

From the knowledge increased by the aforementioned reflection (*manana*), yoga—which is profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*)—proceeds; that is, the perfect knowledge that "nothing exists apart from Brahman" manifests. (19) Thus, the yogi who is constantly devoted to yogic knowledge never perishes, even through the notion of the existence of anything other than himself, just like one who possesses the command (*ājñā*).

The meaning is that, simultaneously with right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), one attains the state of Brahman alone, which is established by the total negation of everything and is devoid of all counter-correlates (*niṣpratiyogika*).
As for the means to right knowledge, it is in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "All this, indeed, is Brahman."

One should perceive Śiva as abiding within all modifications that appear through the perspective of one’s own ignorance. When the realization that "all is Brahman" is thus established, the knowledge arises that nothing whatsoever exists within Śiva apart from the collection of all modifications. Then, the yogi of realized wisdom [perceives] Brahman, which is established as being free from the possibility of any modification.
Having become a possessor of perfect knowledge through the contemplation of nothing else— that "it is one's own nature alone, free from all counterparts"—

one should meditate upon the Self as Brahman alone, which illuminates the yoga of perfect knowledge born from the practice of hearing and so forth as taught by others. Simultaneously with this perfect knowledge consisting of such meditation, [the goal is attained].
The meaning is that one has accomplished what was to be done.
Yoga, which serves as the means to knowledge, does not exist for one who lacks the knowledge of yoga; its state is not accomplished. || 21 ||
Therefore, through the yoga of practice, the yogi should restrain the mind and the vital breaths; he should cut them away as if with a razor of sharpened edge. 22.

The crest-lock is the function consisting of vital breath; through the practice of the eight limbs beginning with restraint (yama), if one does not become qualified for hearing [the scriptures], then neither the knowledge born of yoga nor even the state of perfect knowledge exists for him, even in a dream. Since this is so, therefore—

Thus, through the practice of yoga, the yogi should sever the ignorance that obstructs the attainment of Brahman by means of the razor of the yoga of practice, which possesses a sharpened edge. (22) To the question, "By what means does this yoga of practice arise?", he says: "Instruction," and so forth.

The meaning is that through the practice of the eight-limbed yoga beginning with *yama*, which will be described hereafter, the vital-function known as the "crest of yoga" (*yogaśikhā*), which brings about the fruit of the yoga of practice, comes into being.
The yoga of action and the yoga of knowledge—yoga is considered to be twofold: the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action. || 23 ||
Now, O best of Brahmins, listen to the yoga of action (kriyāyoga), which is the binding of the undisturbed mind to some specific object. (24)
O best of the twice-born, that conjunction is of two kinds: [the first] regarding prescribed actions alone, in the form "this action must be performed. (25)
The constant binding of the mind is called the yoga of action;
whereas the constant binding of the mind to the goal that is the highest good is [yoga]. (26)
That is to be known as the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), which brings about all perfections and is auspicious, for one whose mind is unwavering in both these aforementioned types of yoga. (27)
He attains directly the supreme good characterized by liberation.
He states the extent of that twofold yoga through the distinction between knowledge and action with the words beginning "jñāna" (knowledge).

23. Regarding that, [the passage] beginning with "the yoga of action" (kriyāyoga) and so forth. What is that? It is [the passage] beginning with "of one who is undisturbed" (avyākulasya) and so forth. 24.
Regarding how there is a twofold nature of *kriyā-yoga*, [the text says] "action is to be performed" and so forth.

The meaning is that *karma-yoga* is precisely the dedication to the performance of desireless action with the intention of worshipping the Lord. (25) He states that *jñāna-yoga* is precisely the dedication to the path of the highest good—beginning with the words "But that which... (yattu).
26 || Thus, he says—beginning with "Of whom"—that spiritual welfare arises from the practice of the two-fold yoga consisting of the means (upāya) and the goal (upeya). 27 ||
The eightfold yoga is the means for the knowledge of Brahman without distinction; detachment from the body and the senses is called *yama* by the wise. (28)
Constant devotion to the supreme reality is known as the restraint (niyama);
maintaining an attitude of indifference toward all things is the highest posture (āsana). (29)

This entire world is a false perception; the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa-saṃyama) is the turning of the mind inward, while withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), O best of beings, is that very state. (30)
The steadying of the mind is known as *dhāraṇā* (concentration);
the contemplation that "I am indeed pure consciousness alone" is called *dhyāna* (meditation). || 31 ||
The forgetting of [worldly] meditation is designated as right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
He teaches the eightfold yoga, both concisely and in detail, as the means for attaining the previously mentioned knowledge of Brahman without distinction—beginning with the verse "deha... (28–31).
The ten kinds of restraints and observances are: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, and uprightness. (32)
Forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten restraints (yamas).
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, and the propitiation of Hari [are the observances (niyamas)]. || 33 ||
"Listening to the Vedānta, modesty, intelligence, recitation [of mantras], and vows"— thus it is said.
For those of the highest qualification, the eightfold yoga serves as a means for the knowledge of Brahman.

It has been defined. Regarding that, he says "non-violence" (ahiṃsā) [in verse 32] to show that restraint (yama) is divided tenfold. Likewise, he says "austerity" (tapaḥ) [in verse 33] to show that observance (niyama) is also [divided].
O twice-born one, he spoke of the postures according to the method of Haṭhayoga, as well as their ancillaries such as the Svastika and others.
The svastika mark is described on both soles of the feet; having placed the two knees toward the northeast, this is declared to be the āsana posture. (35)
One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back, and likewise the left ankle on the right side; this is the cow-faced (gomukha) posture, just as the face of a cow is turned.
When one places one foot upon the other thigh and remains motionless,
this is declared to be the Vīrāsana posture, which destroys all sins.
Having restrained the anus with the two ankles in reverse order, one who is composed—this, the knowers of yoga understand, is the yogic posture (yogāsana). || 38 ||
When one places the soles of the feet upon the thighs, this becomes the *padmāsana* (lotus posture), which removes all diseases and poisons. (39)
Having properly established the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should then bind the two big toes with both hands in a reversed manner; thus the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) is formed.

Having properly established the lotus posture (padmāsana) and placed both hands on the ground between the knees and the shins, one should remain standing with the body suspended in the air; this is the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana).
Seated in the cock-posture (kukkuṭāsana), having clasped the neck with both arms, one lies supine like a tortoise; this is the uttānakūrma posture.
Grasping the two big toes with both hands up to the ears,
drawn back like the pull of a bow, is declared the *dhanurāsana* (bow posture).
Pressing the perineum against the region of the ankles in reverse order,
and extending the hands over the knees, this is the lion-form posture (siṃharūpaka).
Having placed both ankles on the ground below the scrotum on either side of the perineum and having secured them with the hands, it becomes the Bhadrāsana posture. (45)
Pressing both the perineum and the sides with the two ankles in reverse order—
this posture is declared to be Muktāsana (the Liberated Posture).
Firmly pressing the ground evenly with the palms of both hands, one should place the elbows at the sides of the navel, like a peacock. (47)
The peacock posture (mayūrāsana) is desired with the head and feet raised;
the right foot is placed at the base of the left thigh, while the hands encircle the knees. 48.
With the left hand, the left big toe is grasped as the "fish-seat" (matsyapīṭhaka);
having pressed the vulva with the left [hand], the right [hand] is placed above the penis. (49)
Seated with the body straight, the Siddhāsana is thus described:
having stretched the two feet upon the ground, one should firmly grasp the two big toes with both hands.
Placing the forehead above the knees is called the western posture (paścima-tāṇa);
by whatever means it may be performed, it results in ease and stability.
That is called the "easy posture" (sukhāsana); one who is unable [to perform other postures] should practice that.
By him by whom the posture is conquered, the three worlds are conquered. 52.

Now, for those of middling capacity, he teaches the ancillaries such as the postures (*āsana*) according to the method of *haṭhayoga*: "The postures... (34). Among these, he states the definition of the *svastika* posture:
"It is described... (35). The definition of the *gomukha* posture is stated: "The left... (36).
He describes the characteristics of *vīrāsana*—[verse 37]. He clarifies the characteristics of *yogāsana*.
He elucidates the characteristics of *baddhapadmāsana*: "Having bound with both hands"—that which is so described becomes *baddhapadmāsana*. [Verse 40]. The manner of *kukkuṭāsana*...
He clarifies this with the word "lotus" (padma). He states the characteristic of the upward-facing tortoise with the words "cock" (kukkuṭa) and so forth.
42 || He states the *anurāsana* [supplementary posture]: "With the feet... || 43 || He demonstrates the *siṃhāsana* [lion posture]: "The *sīvinī*... || 44 ||
He describes the characteristics of the Bhadrāsana: "the two ankles... (45). He describes the nature of the Muktāsana:
"the sīvinī... (46). He describes the method for Mayūrāsana: "having supported... (47).

He describes the characteristics of the Matsyāsana posture: "vāma... (verse 48). He states the characteristics of the Siddhāsana posture: [omitted]. He describes the posture suitable for those who are unable [to perform the others]: "yena... (verse 51). He states the fruit of the postures: "āsanam... (verse 52).
The Procedure for Breath Control (Prāṇāyāma) Preceded by the Purification of the Channels:

Being well-restrained by means of the restraints (yamas), the observances (niyamas), and the postures (āsanas), and having first performed the purification of the channels, one should practice breath control. (53)
The measurement of the body is ninety-six finger-breadths in length according to one's own fingers;
the vital breath (prāṇa) extends twelve finger-breadths beyond the body.
One who, through yoga, makes the wind residing in the body— whether diminished or equalized— harmonious with the fire produced within the body, is recognized as a knower of Brahman.

He describes the sequence of *prāṇāyāma* for the yogi distinguished by the three limbs beginning with *yama*, preceded by the purification of the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*), starting with the words "By the *yamas*," etc.; [this refers to] those previously mentioned. (53)
Regarding the measure of the body and vital breath (prāṇa) conducive to practice, he states the result of that practice of the vital breath [in verses 54–55]:
"The measure of the body... and so forth.
The nature of the fire-mandala is the place of the flame in the center of the body, possessing the luster of molten gold;
it is triangular for bipeds, and otherwise quadrangular for quadrupeds. (56)
The abode of birds is circular, that of those born from eggs is hexagonal, and that of those born from sweat is octagonal; therein it shines like a lamp.
(p. 133) He explains the nature of the mandala of the root-fire with the words "the body" (deha). || 56 ||
The meaning is: know that within each of those circles of living beings, there is a blazing fire. || 57 ||
The location of the navel is the location of the *kanda*, situated nine finger-breadths from the center of the human body;
it is four finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in length. (58)
The egg-shaped form belongs to birds, oviparous creatures, and quadrupeds;
that [form] is indeed desired as having the belly in the middle, and its center is considered to be the navel.
He clarifies the interior of the human body and so forth with the words beginning "kanda" (verse 58–59).
The living soul wanders within the wheel of channels;
therein is a twelve-spoked wheel, upon which reside the forms of Viṣṇu and the other deities.
I am situated there and cause the wheel to revolve by means of my own māyā.
O best of the twice-born, the living being wanders through the spokes in succession, just as a spider moves within the midst of its web of threads. (61)
The individual soul (jīva) moves mounted upon the vital breath (prāṇa), for it cannot exist without it;

and the wheel of channels (nāḍī-cakra) situated therein functions while presided over by Viṣṇu and the other deities. Regarding this, he says "therein" (tatra): "Therein, abiding as the inner controller (antaryāmin) through my own self, I set that [wheel] in motion. Therein—
In the center of the navel is the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra).
O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the region of the heart of all beings,
causing all beings to revolve by means of His illusory power (māyā), as if they were mounted on a machine.

Thus, in accordance with the Smṛti, [it says] "I" and so forth. To the question, "By whom are you made to wander? he replies: the *lūtikā* is a spider, a specific kind of insect; likewise, the *jīva* (individual soul) undergoes movement—this is the meaning.
The location of Kuṇḍalinī and her function: above that, the location of Kuṇḍalinī is transverse to the navel and also above it. (62)
She, whose form consists of the eight primal elements, is coiled eightfold;
she constantly directs the movement of the vital breaths as well as water, food, and so forth, exactly as they ought to be.
Having completely blocked the sides of the *kanda*, she remains always stationed there;
likewise, she completely envelops the opening of the *brahmarandhra* with her mouth.
Awakened by the wind together with fire at the time of yoga,
she vibrates within the space of the heart, radiant and great, in the form of a serpent.
He describes the location of the Kuṇḍalinī that shines above that, as well as its function, with the words "of that" (tasya).
[This refers to] that wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra). || 62 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind,
intellect, and ego— thus is my nature divided eightfold.

According to the traditional Smṛti, the meaning is that she exists in the form of the eightfold primordial nature (*aṣṭaprakṛti*), which is the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*) and the unification of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. [Regarding the question] "What does she do while remaining?", [the answer is] "By means of the mouth alone," and so forth. [Regarding the question] "When does she flow upwards?", [the answer is] "At the time of yoga," and so forth.
The nature of the root-tube (nāḍīkanda) situated in the middle of the body is two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis;
for humans, this is the center of the body, whereas for quadrupeds, it is the center of the heart.
p. 135) For others, the middle of the abdomen is surrounded by various channels;
within the center of the body, which is joined with the fourfold [channels], there is the Suṣumṇā. || 67 ||
Situated in the middle of the bulb (kanda), the Suṣumṇā channel is well-established;
resembling the fiber of a lotus stalk, it is straight and extends upwards.
Extending as far as the aperture of Brahmā, marked by the flashing of lightning, is the Vaiṣṇavī channel, the path for attaining Nirvāṇa. || 69 ||
Iḍā and Piṅgalā are situated on its left and right respectively;
Iḍā, originating from the kanda, extends as far as the left nostril. (70)
And from that [place], Piṅgalā has arisen, extending to the right nostril;
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā, as well as two other channels, are situated there. (71)
In front of and behind her, toward her left and right eyes,
the two channels Pūṣā and Yaśasvinī arise from that very place.
The auspicious channel called Avalambusā extends from the base of the anus to the limit of the left ear; it descends and reaches as far as the penis.
Extending from the big toe down to the *kanda*, the *kauśikī* flows below;
these ten types of channels are said to originate from the *kanda*.
Rooted in that [central channel] are many channels, both gross and subtle.
There are seventy-two thousand channels, both gross and subtle. (75)
They cannot be numbered at all—those various types with thick roots—just as subtle and thick fibers are spread out upon the leaf of an ashvattha tree. (76)
He describes the nature of the *kanda*—the root of the channels that serve as the support for that [body]—in the words "from the *apāna*" and so forth.

66–67. Regarding this, what is this principal channel (*pradhānanāḍī*), and depending upon it, how many channels exist? To this it is said: "The *kanda*... [etc. Relying on the neck of the lute (*vīṇādaṇḍa*), it extends straight upward. (68) As for how far it extends upward, he says: "up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). [69]

Regarding "the aperture of Brahmā" (*brahmarandhra*): the meaning is that it extends from the *mūlādhāra* up to the aperture of Brahmā. He specifies its name as "Vaiṣṇavī," because it is presided over by Viṣṇu. It is called the "Brahma-nāḍī" because it leads to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*).
The *kaivalya-nāḍī* contained within that is the path for attaining *nirvāṇa*, because it is the track leading to absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). || 69 ||
The channels that serve as its support are stated: "and the *iḍā*" (vv. 70–75). He provides an illustration for their being innumerable: "just as" (v. 76).
The winds moving within the channels are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 77 ||
The ten vital winds, beginning with prāṇa, move within the ten channels;
among them, the pentad beginning with prāṇa is primary, and within that, two are preeminent. (78)
Alternatively, Prāṇa alone is the eldest, for it sustains the individual soul (jīvātman) within the middle of the mouth and nose, the heart, and the region of the navel.
(137) O best of the twice-born, the big toe of the foot is a station of the *prāṇa*; the *apāna*, O Brahmin, moves through the anus, the penis, the thighs, and the knees. (80)
The *samāna* wind is established as all-pervading throughout all the limbs;
the *udāna* wind resides in all the joints, as well as in the feet and the hands.
Vyāna is located in the ears, thighs, and hips, as well as in the ankles, shoulders, and throat;
the five winds beginning with Nāga are situated in the skin, bones, and other such parts. 82.
The water, food, and the [five] tastes and so forth, once they have been made uniform within the belly, the *prāṇa* situated in the middle of the belly shall separate them individually. (83)
The prāṇa, existing separately, performs such activities as these;
and the apāna wind effects the discharge of urine and so forth. (84)
The activities of the prāṇa, apāna, and other vital breaths are sustained by the vyāna wind;
the body is animated by the udāna wind. (85)
The *samāna* wind always performs the nourishment and other functions of the body;
*nāga* produces belching and other such actions, while *kūrma* effects the closing of the eyes and so forth. (86)
Kṛkara is the agent of the two nights; Datta is said to perform the functions of sleep and so forth;
and Dhanañjaya is declared to be the beauty and other qualities of the dead body. (87)
Regarding the question of how many winds move within the channels (*nāḍī*), [the answer begins with] "prāṇa and apāna," and so forth. (77)

To the question of which among them is the primary one, he says: "prāṇa and so forth" (verse 78). He points out their locations: "in the mouth" and so on (verses 79–82). He describes the functions of prāṇa and the others: "situated in the belly" and so on (verses 83–86). Regarding the two "kṣapas," these refer to the closing and opening of the eyes (verse 87).

(138) O best of the twice-born, the purification of the channels is preceded by the knowledge of the channels; having thus understood the divisions of the channels, the divisions of the vital winds, the very locations of those winds, and their various movements— 88. O best of the twice-born, the purification of the channels is preceded by the knowledge of the channels; having thus understood the divisions of the channels, the divisions of the vital winds, the very locations of those winds, and their various movements—
"One should strive for the purification of the channels, endowed with the previously mentioned knowledge.
Thus, having understood the distinctions, locations, and so forth of the channels, he says "the channels" [in verse 88] to indicate that one should strive for their purification.
Regarding the place for the practice of yoga and its procedure: having resorted to a secluded spot, one should remain free from all worldly attachments. (89)
There, upon an auspicious wooden seat prepared with *darbha* grass, *kuśa* grass, a black antelope skin, and other materials, complete with the substances required for the limbs of yoga, [he sat].
The seat should be of such height and such a width of two [cubits], and having sat properly upon it—such as the svastika posture or whatever is preferred—one should remain. (91)
He describes the locus of yoga and the procedure for yoga, beginning with the verse "vivikta... (89–91).
O Brahmin, having performed the kevala-kumbhaka accompanied by the cin-mudrā, one should first assume the posture with the body straight and the mind concentrated;
the eyes fixed on the tip of the nose and the teeth not touching the teeth. (92)
Placing the tongue against the palate, with a mind established in its own nature and free from affliction, slightly contracting the head and binding it with the yoga-mudrā. (93)
One should perform *prāṇāyāma* with the hands according to the prescribed method. (p.
139) He prepares the introductory context for explaining the characteristics of *prāṇāyāma* with the words "having bound," etc.
The meaning of "yoga-mudrā" is the binding of the nose or the three bindings (*bandha*). 92.
The meaning is that one should perform the kevala-kumbhaka breath control.
Prāṇāyāma with retention consists of the exhalation of air, the inhalation [of air], and likewise the purification through exhalation. || 94 ||
The control of breath (*prāṇāyāma*) is declared to consist of four [steps] for the purification of the vital air (*vāyu*).
He states the definition of *sahita-prāṇāyāma* as follows: "Exhalation... (verse 94).

At the time of beginning *prāṇāyāma*, the expulsion of the vitiated air from the body, followed by its filling, then the purification of the air through retention (*kumbhaka*), and finally its complete expulsion— this affliction of the air through these four cycles is declared to be the introductory *prāṇāyāma*.
Thus, when the three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) have been performed, the meaning is that the body then becomes fit for the practice of breath-restraint as previously described.
The breath control for purifying the channels:
one should press the nostril with the right hand alone. || 95 ||
Then, one should gradually expel the piṅgalā wind from the outside;
O Brahmin, having filled the breath through the iḍā with sixteen mātrās.
After filling [the breath], one should then perform kumbhaka for sixty-four mātrās;
one should properly exhale the piṅgalā-breath for thirty-two mātrās.
In this manner, one should perform the practice again and again, both in reverse and in direct order;
one should then restrain the body with the vital air (mātariśvan) like a full jar.
O Brahmin, when all the channels are filled by the vital air (mātariśvan) in this manner,
the ten winds circulate.
The lotus of the heart also clearly becomes fully blossomed;
there one should behold the Supreme Self, Vāsudeva, who is stainless. (100)
One should practice breath-retentions (kumbhaka) four times a day— at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight— gradually increasing up to eighty repetitions each time.
By practicing it for even a single day, one is liberated from all sins;
after three years, a man becomes devoted solely to *prāṇāyāma*.
The yogi who has mastered yoga becomes a conqueror of the vital breaths and a subduer of the senses;
eating little and sleeping little, he becomes radiant and powerful. (103)
Having averted untimely death, one shall attain a long life.

The sequence of breath control (prāṇāyāma) to be practiced for the purpose of purifying the channels is stated as follows: "With the hand," etc. The procedure, however, is: having filled [the lungs] through the *iḍā* and retained the breath (*kumbhita*), one performs exhalation (*recana*) through the *piṅgalā*.
As for the *vyutkrama* (reverse order): having filled [the breath] through *piṅgalā* and retained it (*kumbhita*), one performs exhalation (*recana*) through *iḍā*. 95–97.
Thus, day by day, four times a day, preceded by an increase of one *mātrā* per day, one should practice eighty *prāṇāyāmas*; so he says: "completely," etc. 98–99. *Vyākoca*.
Expansion. || 100-103 ||
He for whom the fruit of breath control is merely the production of perspiration during his practices of prāṇāyāma is the lowest. || 104 ||
He whose body trembles during the middle breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) is the middling;
he whose body rises up is declared to be the best.

In the lowest [grade], there shall be the destruction of diseases and sins; in the middling, moreover, the destruction of sins, diseases, and great maladies; and in the highest, furthermore, [the same]. || 106 ||
He has scant urine and scant feces, a light body, and moderate eating;
his senses are keen, his intellect is sharp, he knows the three periods of time, and he possesses self-mastery. (107)
For one who, having abandoned exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), performs only the retention of breath (kumbhaka) at the three times of day, there is nothing that is difficult to attain.
Regarding the attainment of results such as perspiration, trembling, and rising [from the ground] at the time of initial practice, he says:
"The accomplishment of desired objects shall occur"—thus he states "the exhalation" (recaka). || 108 ||

Through the retention of breath (prāṇadhāraṇā), disease is destroyed; one who is diligent should, by means of the mind, retain the vital breaths at the navel-center, the tip of the nose, and the big toe, either during the periods of twilight or always.
Freed from all diseases and devoid of fatigue, the yogi shall live;
by fixing [the breath] upon the navel-knots, there shall be the destruction of diseases of the abdomen.
From the practice of concentration on the tip of the nose, there shall be long life and lightness of the body;
when the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, one should draw in the breath through the tongue.
By drinking [it] for three months, great accomplishment of speech shall arise;
and by practicing it for six months, there is the destruction of major diseases. (112)
Wherever the wind is held within a limb afflicted by disease or other ailments, through that very concentration on the vital air (marut), one attains health in each respective part. || 113 ||

(142) He states that by holding the vital air (*vāyu*) in whichever limb is afflicted by disease, there shall be an increase in longevity through the cessation of that specific ailment—beginning with "the navel" (*nābhi*) and so forth. This refers to the yogi who has attained mastery through the practice of *kevala-kumbhaka*. (109–113)
Through the six-faced mudrā, there is mastery over the mind;
by the very concentration (*dhāraṇā*) of the mind, the vital air (*pavana*) becomes concentrated.
O best of the twice-born, the cause for the stabilization of the mind is now stated. (114)
Having withdrawn the organs from their objects and being composed, one should draw the *apāna* upward and hold it above the abdomen. || 115 ||
Binding with both hands the organs of sense, such as the ears and so forth, according to their proper order,
he brings his mind under his own control while practicing by the path previously described.
By means of the mind, the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) is always brought under one's own control.

Because of the inseparable relationship between the mind and the vital breath, he demonstrates the Ṣaṇmukhī-mudrā for the purpose of mastering the mind—beginning with the words "of the mind" (manasaḥ). What is that? It begins with the words "the causes" (kāraṇāni), and so forth. || 114–116 ||
He says, "The mind," explaining that through the power of the mind, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) also comes under one's own control.
The movement of the vital breath consists in the breath flowing alternately through the two nostrils. || 117 ||
And within those three channels,
as long as this vital breath (prāṇa) moves through the southern opening of the Śaṅkhinī for the sake of living beings, it sustains them.
Furthermore, for that same duration of time, he moves continuously in the gentle [channel].
He explains the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as follows: "The nose," etc. (117).
Beginning from the *mūlādhāra* and ending at the center of the eyebrows, there are three [channels] distinguished as *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and so forth; thus it is said.

There are three channels distinguished by *iḍā* and the others. Among those, the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *suṣumnā* occurs only for those who are yogins among living beings. However, for non-yogins, this [movement]— [Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete.]

The *prāṇa* moves for as long as it lasts through the right nostril—the right nasal cavity—known as *piṅgalā*, which is like a conch shell (*śaṅkha*) characterized by three internal spirals. This is the *śaṅkhinī*.
118 || Furthermore, for that same duration, it moves through the left nostril;
thus, the meaning is that the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs continuously in both the Piṅgalā and the Iḍā.
Through the knowledge of the movement of the vital breath, yoga is attained; thus, by means of the wind moving in this sequence, a person becomes a conqueror of wind.
Having understood day and night, the fortnight, the month, the solstice, and so forth, one who is concentrated and inward-turned should discern the divisions of time.
Even by the non-vibration or non-perception of one's own limbs, such as the big toe and so forth,
through these omens (ariṣṭas), one should know the exhaustion of one's own life.
Having understood this, the best among the knowers of yoga should strive for the attainment of absolute liberation (kaivalya),
when the throbbing in his big toes and big fingers ceases.
For such a person, after one year has passed, their life will come to an end;
likewise, for one whose throbbing in the wrist and the ankle ceases.
The duration of this person's life shall be limited to six months;
for one whose elbow throbs, the duration is three months. (124)
(144) If throbbing is not perceived in the armpits or at the sides of the genitals, one's life shall last for a month; if [throbbing] is seen in living beings, it shall be half of that. 125.
The life of one whose light is like that of a firefly, residing within the door of the belly for ten days, is truly his life. (126)
If the tip of the tongue is not visible, one's own stay [in this world] lasts for three days;
if it is seen with a flame, death certainly occurs within two days. (127)
Having observed such omens as these, which are the causes for the exhaustion of life, one should apply oneself to the highest good, devoted to the practice of recitation and meditation. || 128 ||
Having meditated upon the Supreme Self with the mind, one attains its very nature.

If the yogi thus becomes a knower of the movement of the vital breath (*vāyu*), then, having understood the course of his own life-span in accordance with the science of sounds (*svara-śāstra*), he swiftly applies his mind toward the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

Having known the Supreme Self—which is established through the negation of non-self—to be one's own self alone, one should become absorbed in that state; thus he says: "In this way," etc. (vv. 119–120).
He states the means for knowing the distinction of time with the words beginning "the big toe" (aṅguṣṭha) etc.
(verse 121). He himself explains his own statement with the words "the big toe of the foot" (pādāṅguṣṭha) etc. (verses 122–128).
The withdrawal of the vital breath (prāṇa) into the vital points (marmasthāna); that is, its retention within the eighteen types of vital points. || 129 ||
Drawing [the breath] from one place to another is called pratyāhāra;
likewise, [it involves drawing it] to the big toe, the ankle, and the middle of the shank. (130)
The roots of the two thighs, the anus, the heart, the genitals, the middle of the body, the navel, and the throat and elbow; 131.
The root of the palate, the root of the nose, the circle of the eyes, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, the crown of the head, and the two knees. (132)
O twice-born one, these indeed are the great [points], namely the root and the roots of the hands.

He describes the method of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) with the words "yadi" (if). As to which are the vital points (marmasthāna), he says "pādāṅguṣṭham" (the big toe of the foot); [this refers to] the eighteen locations beginning with the big toe of the foot.
The meaning is that one should withdraw the vital breath (prāṇa) by means of the sequence of ascending and descending. || 130-132 ||
The method of concentration (dhāraṇā) [is practiced] upon these five elements within the body, which consists of the five elements. || 133 ||

That which is the holding of the mind by one disciplined through restraint (yama) and the other [observances] is concentration (dhāraṇā), and it is the cause for crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra. 134.
He describes the method of concentration (dhāraṇā) both briefly and in detail:
"In the five elements, which have been clearly distinguished... (133–134).
Regarding the retention of the five elements within the limbs of the body: from the knees down to the feet, the locus of earth is prescribed;
it is yellow, square, and marked with a vajra. (135)
Five ghaṭikās should be understood there as the place for applying the wind;
the location of the waters is proclaimed to extend from the knees up to the hips. (136)
Having mounted the ten channels of breath upon water, one should remember the white [moon], shaped like a half-moon and marked with the sign of Arjuna. 137.
p. 146) The location of the fire is said to extend from the beginning of the body to its very end.
Therein, the fire is the color of vermilion and blazes with fifteen [flames]. (138)
One should contemplate the *ghaṭikā* (the breath-cycle) by making the *prāṇa* the object of meditation within the *kumbha* (the retention);
indeed, the locus of the wind is there, from above the navel up to the tip of the nose.

The powerful wind of the elements, smoky in color and shaped like a railing, should be brought to mind by means of the *kumbhaka* [retention] after having fixed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within that wind. 140.
From that nose up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila), there are twenty ghaṭikās;
there lies the station of space (vyomasthāna), which is the sky, possessing a luster like crushed collyrium.

Having established the vital air (māruta) in the ether through the practice of breath-retention (kumbhaka), the diligent practitioner performs the dhāraṇā of the five elements—earth and the rest—upon the various parts of his own body. He describes that result [as follows]:
"Mastery over the five elements and their derivatives. The meaning is that even death does not exist therein.
He states the sequence for holding [the breath] starting from the abdomen: "From the knees... (136–141).

Regarding the earth and the other elements, there is the meditation on Aniruddha and others and its fruit; specifically, in the aspect of earth, one visualizes the body with four arms and a crown. (142)
The yogi should strive for liberation from worldly existence by means of Hari, who is unceasing; the yogi of exalted intellect should fulfill Nārāyaṇa within the non-lineage (abaṃśa). 143.
One should always remember Pradyumna in the fire element, Saṃkarṣaṇa in the portion of air, and Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self, in the portion of ether. 144.
There is no doubt that for one who practices yoga, the attainment of that [state] occurs before long.
Having first performed the *dhāraṇā* on the five elements in this manner,
he says— beginning with "Earth" (verse 142)— that one should then meditate upon Aniruddha and the others within the respective portions of earth and the other elements.

Having first assumed a yogic posture, one should fix the meditation on the Supreme Self and its fruit; then, placing the palms together in the heart-center, one should perform the heart-añjali. || 145 ||
With his eyes fixed on the tip of the nose, having placed the tongue against the palate, not touching the teeth with the teeth, with the body erect and composed; 146.
One should restrain the collection of the senses through pure self-awareness by means of meditating upon Vāsudeva, the supreme and highest Self. (147)
Meditation on the nature of one's own essential form bestows the attainment of liberation;
he who, by means of breath-retention (kumbhaka), contemplates Vāsudeva for even a single watch (yāma) [attains this]. 148.
The sin accumulated over seven lifetimes of that yogin is destroyed.
He describes the means for meditating upon the Supreme Self and its fruit, beginning with the words "having bound" (baddhvā).
(Verses 145–147) Thus, he states the intermediate result of meditation, beginning with the words "for only a watch" (yāmamātram). (Verse 148) [Sin...]
The three types of karma, beginning with that which is to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), are indicated by that [term].
The consciousness of Vāsudeva, which transcends the fourth state (turiyatita), begins from the root of the navel and extends as far as the region of the heart. || 149 ||

One should know that the waking state resides in the throat, the dreaming state in the throat as well, the deep sleep state is situated in the middle of the palate, and the fourth state (turiya) is established between the eyebrows. 150.

One should perceive the supreme Brahman, which transcends the fourth state (turyātīta), within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); [this perception] begins from the waking state and extends as far as the interior of the cavity of Brahmā. (151)
In that context, this Self is the fourth (turiya); at the end of the fourth, Viṣṇu is spoken of.

Anticipating the objection that [the state] beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is distinct from Vāsudeva, [the author] first demonstrates the stage beyond the fourth, showing that it is indeed the consciousness of Vāsudeva himself.

He says it is "beyond the fourth" (turyātīta) with the words "at the navel" (nābhī). || 149 || The meaning is that because of the realization of its non-occurrence at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and other locations, the Viṣṇu-tattva is indeed beyond the fourth alone, and nothing else. || 150–151 ||
One who is fully engaged in meditation with qualities should practice saguṇa-dhyāna within the utterly pure sky.
Or one should meditate upon Adhokṣaja, who possesses the brilliance of ten million suns, who is eternally risen,
seated within the lotus of the heart, and whose form is the universe.
Adorned with many forms, endowed with many faces, joined with many arms, and decorated with many weapons. || 154 ||
The god who wears various colors, both peaceful and fierce, with uplifted weapons, filled with many eyes, and possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns. (155)
For the yogi who meditates, all mental fluctuations perish.
He describes the method of meditation with and without attributes [in verse 152]: "By means of meditation...
[verse 152]. Or, one should meditate upon the Virāj, whose form is the universe, inlaid with manifold shapes [verse 153].
The meaning is that it consists of both the stable and the moving. (154–155) He states the fruit of meditating on the state of Vairāja:
because it has reached its ultimate consummation, the mind, having abandoned its nature as mind, becomes the very state of Vairāja; this is the meaning.
The meditation on the qualityless [Brahman] is the imperishable light of consciousness situated in the center of the heart-lotus. (156)
Having the form of a kadamba bud, it is beyond the fourth state (turyātīta),
higher than the highest, infinite, consisting of bliss, composed of consciousness, luminous, and all-pervading.
For that yogi who meditates on [the Self] which is like a lamp in a windless place and like the luster of an uncut gem, liberation rests in the palm of his hand. 158.

He describes the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇadhyāna) with the word "in the heart" (hṛt). It is "situated in the middle of the heart-lotus" because it abides there in the form of immediate presence. To avoid the contingency of insentience due to its connection with the heart, it is described as the "light of consciousness. To avoid the contingency of its destruction due to the destruction of its support, [it is described as]...

"Imperishable" (avyayam) || 156 || That which has the form of a *kadamba* cluster is "shaped like a *kadamba* cluster," referring to the thousand-spoked [lotus]. According to the scriptural statement that "the fourth is situated at the crown of the head," it is indeed appropriate that the Fourth (*turīya*), as it is perceived there, possesses that same shape. This is the meaning.
In the absence of those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that very state is *turīyātīta* (beyond the fourth), even more transcendent than the supreme *turīya*;

it is infinite because of the absence of the three types of limitation—according to the Śruti, Brahman is devoid of limitation in terms of space, time, and substance; it is "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) because its essential nature is supreme bliss.

It is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), because it is pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*). It is the Sun (*bhāskara*), because even the lights ranging from fireflies to the sun take on their luminous form by reflecting it. From the perspective of the wise, it becomes nothing but Brahman;
thus, it is all-pervading (*vibhu*). It is like a lamp in a windless place, because it is as motionless as space.
The meaning is that it is pure luminosity, possessing the radiance of natural jewels such as the Kaustubha.

For the yogi who meditates upon Brahmana, characterized by such attributes, with the realization that it is nothing but his own Self— for him who meditates thus, liberation, that is, disembodied liberation (videhamukti), is held in the palm of his hand.
The meaning is: because of having attained that state. || 158 ||
Even knowledge with its specific distinctions is a cause of liberation:
"For whatever form of the God whose nature is the universe— whether gross,
subtle, or otherwise— one beholds within the lotus of the heart," (159).
For the yogin who meditates, that which manifests directly indeed brings about the fruits such as *aṇimā* with ease. (160)
If it is thus for both the individual soul and the Supreme as well, then the established state is:
"I alone am the Supreme Brahman; I am Brahman. (161)
That samādhi, however, should be known as being devoid of all mental fluctuations;
the yogi attains Brahman and shall not enter into worldly existence again. || 162 ||
Having thus purified the principles with a mind free from desire, the yogi becomes like a fire without fuel, which subsides by itself. (163)
In the absence of an object of perception, the mind and vital breath, conjoined with determinative knowledge,
the individual soul merges into the supreme pure reality like a lump of salt.
He perceives the entire universe, a dense mass of the web of delusion, as if in a dream;
he who moves like one in deep sleep, utterly unmoved by his own nature. (165)
Relying upon the state of nirvana, the yogi attains absolute liberation.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

Anticipating the objection that liberation belongs only to one who possesses knowledge of the featureless (nirviśeṣa) and not to one who possesses knowledge of the qualified (saviśeṣa), he states—beginning with "viśvarūpaśca"—that since knowledge of the qualified is the cause of knowledge of the featureless, its status as a cause of liberation is also established. [The result is] the powers such as atomization (aṇimā). || 159 ||
The meaning is "of one who has desire. If he were free from desire, then for him there would be the non-conceptual samādhi on Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self. || 160 ||

He also states the characteristic of samādhi: "jīva" etc. To refute the resulting notions of non-Brahmanhood and non-Selfhood, and for the sake of awakening to their identity, one should meditate through mutual exchange (*vyatihāra*) in the form of the Brahman non-different from the inner self (*pratyag-abhinna-brahma-rūpa*), thinking: "I alone am the Supreme Brahman; Brahman am I."
p. 151) The state of non-conceptual samādhi characterized by non-cognition (*asaṃprajñāta-nirvikalpa-samādhi*).

Thus, through the power of non-conceptual samādhi, there is established the realization that no specific attributes can possibly exist within Brahman—which is non-different from the inner self (*pratyak*) and independent of anything external (*parāk*).
One attains Brahman. || 161–162 || Regarding the question "By what means does one attain Brahman?", the answer is:
"In this manner. The meaning is that one attains Brahman with a mind free from longing for anything other than oneself.
Simultaneously with the awakening to Brahman alone—which is non-dual and devoid of any counter-correlate—even if only as a mere appearance—of the mind... [the state is realized].
If there is the delusion that "the collection of organs exists," then its cessation would occur;
thus he speaks with an illustration, beginning with "yathā" (just as). It is "praśāmyate," meaning it becomes tranquil. Why?

Because in the absence of any object of perception apart from itself, the individual soul (*jīva*), which is conditioned by the adjunct of *prāṇa*, merges into the Supreme Pure Being (*śuddhasattva*).
The meaning is that, like a lump of salt in water, having abandoned the state of being a living soul (jīva), one becomes Brahman.
164 || If there were the manifestation of a universe separate from oneself, then delusion would exist in that manifestation, and so forth.
But when that does not manifest, he who moves about like one in deep sleep is perfectly steady in his own nature. 165 ||

That which is the abiding as the non-dual Brahman alone—which is established through the negation of the manifestation of the universe as something separate from oneself—is the state of *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the meaning is that the yogi of the knowledge of Brahman alone remains in the form of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) simultaneously with that knowledge. This concludes the word "Upaniṣad."
This marks the conclusion of the Triśikhibrāhmaṇopaniṣad.
The commentary on the present Upaniṣad has been written clearly and concisely by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The commentary on the relevant Upaniṣad consists of three hundred and sixty [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Triśikhibrāhmaṇopaniṣad, constituting the forty-fourth work in the venerable exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
